 Live .  10,759 viewing 10759 viewing Live page Updated 1 minute ago China's Xi greets Trump at airport in rare move ahead of trilateral talks with Putin
 Summary
 China's Xi Jinping welcomes US President Donald Trump to Shenzhen with a hug on the tarmac - a carefully choreographed moment of flattery, writes our correspondent 
 It comes ahead of a historic trilateral meeting between the two leaders and Russia's Vladimir Putin, taking place on Thursday
 Xi earlier welcomed Putin to China, calling him an "old friend". Our Russia editor says some local newspapers are already calling this visit a "diplomatic victory" for Putin - simply because it's happening 
 China is hosting a summit of Asia Pacific leaders in Shenzhen, a booming hub for manufacturing and advanced tech 
 Meanwhile, Trump arrives from the Philippines where he attended another summit - images show him meeting India's Narendra Modi, Australia's Anthony Albanese and Japan's Sanae Takaichi

 Live Reporting
 Edited by Tinshui Yeung, with Laura Bicker, Steve Rosenberg and Stephen McDonell in China and Nada Tawfik travelling with President Trump
 Putin and Trump 'will meet a few times' at summit - Kremlin senior aide published at 10:21 GMT 10:21 GMT 
 Laura Gozzi 
Europe reporter 
 Image source, Getty Images Kremlin senior aide Yury Ushakov has said Putin and Trump - who are due to meet Xi Jinping tomorrow - could meet at tonight's gala dinner.
 "And they will definitely meet tomorrow," Ushakov adds in comments to Russian state TV. "Both during the plenary session of the Apec summit and immediately after it concludes."
 "The leaders will meet, believe me, and they will have a substantive conversation, regardless of where they happen to be sitting - in armchairs, on chairs or on stools - or standing face-to-face, looking each other in the eye. The meeting will take place. Our president and the US president will meet a few times over the course of the summit," Ushakov says.
 He also hints the meeting could take place on the sidelines of the summit, without the presence of large delegations.

 Historic Xi-Trump-Putin meeting reportedly to take place at a villa published at 10:12 GMT 10:12 GMT 
 BBC Chinese 
 Image source, AFP via Getty Images The trilateral meeting between China, the US and Russia is reportedly set to take place at Kylin Villa in Shenzhen on Thursday, with security significantly tightened ahead of the talks.
 The state-owned compound, which opened in 1997, has long hosted Chinese leaders and high-profile foreign visitors to the city.
 Beijing’s decision to opt for a more private setting rather than a formal conference venue suggests the meeting is “more of a sideline rather than a separate, significant summit on its own”, says Minseon Ku of DePaul University, a specialist in summit diplomacy.
 “Xi would want that, since, as the host of Apec, China would want the Apec summit to be the primary event and would not want the trilateral meeting to overshadow it,” she tells the BBC.
 Professor Shaoyu Yuan of New York University, who studies US-China diplomacy, notes that Kylin Villa is relatively easy to secure. Its proximity to the airport would also allow Trump to depart directly after the meeting.
 "The setting carries less diplomatic formality than an official venue in Beijing, framing the roughly one-hour meeting as a working-level engagement. The lower the ceremonial profile, the lower the political cost if the meeting produces no tangible outcomes," he says.

 Nvidia spy scandal looming over Trump and Xi meeting published at 09:57 GMT 09:57 GMT 
 Laura Bicker 
China correspondent 
 Image source, AFP via Getty Images Jensen Huang is out as CEO of Nvidia, but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping.
 The allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with businesswoman Alice Huang - who US officials suspect of being a Chinese spy - are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship.
 Beijing's foreign ministry described the spy claims as a "smear against China", and Chinese officials worry this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech.
 Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms accessing advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. Beijing has called the new rules "economic coercion". 
 The Nvidia scandal may spiral into something bigger for US-China ties.

 Taiwan demands participation on 'equal basis' published at 09:40 GMT 09:40 GMT 
 Benny Lu 
BBC Chinese 
 Apec is one of the few international bodies of which Taiwan is a formal member – the self-governed island is in fact a founding member – and its attendance at the leaders' summit usually goes fairly smoothly. 
 This year's gathering in China, however, has introduced complications because of tensions with Beijing. 
 China says it welcomes Taiwan's participation under the "one-China principle", which asserts that Taiwan is not an independent territory but a part of China. But Taipei has rejected this, with President William Lai saying last week that Taiwan's participation should be regarded on an "equal basis".
 "Apec is different because Taiwan already enjoys formal membership," Felix Brender, a postdoctoral fellow in Taiwan studies at Harvard, says, arguing that it'll be hard for Beijing to challenge Taipei's participation – unlike in the cases of the UN and the World Health Organisation, where Taiwan is not officially recognised.

 Takaichi arrived in Shenzhen earlier amid frosty Japan-China ties published at 09:29 GMT 09:29 GMT 
 Image source, Getty Images Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also arrived in Shenzhen a little earlier.
 This is Takaichi's first official visit to China since taking office in October 2025 - and comes as relations between the two countries have fallen to the lowest point in over a decade.
 A row erupted between Tokyo and Beijing in November last year, when Takaichi appeared to suggest that Japan could activate its self-defence force in the event of an attack on Taiwan, a self-governed island which China claims as its own.
 This set off a war of words, then led to trade and export restrictions.
 Analysts believe formal talks between Takaichi and Xi on the sidelines of Apec are unlikely, although they may have a brief exchange such as a handshake.

 This is no ordinary welcome published at 09:24 GMT 09:24 GMT 
 Laura Bicker 
Reporting from Shenzhen 
 This isn’t simply an airport greeting by Chinese President Xi Jinping. This is a carefully choreographed diplomatic moment.
 Xi understands the value of this gesture, as it is thought to be the first time that he has greeted a foreign leader at the airport as President.
 Firstly, he is mirroring Trump’s own actions. 
 The US president was there to meet Xi at the airport in Washington earlier this year - and now the Chinese leader is returning the compliment.
 But Xi will also be aware that Trump places considerable importance on personal recognition, ceremony and status. 
 By not delegating this task, the Chinese president is flattering his US counterpart and making him feel important by singling him out for the honour of a personal greeting.
 Xi may hope that this sign of good will smooth the path for negotiations over trade, Taiwan and technology. 
 He can also afford to be gracious here without losing face. China is already controlling the setting and arrangement for the unprecedented summit between Trump, Xi and Putin.

 Chinese citizens gather to welcome Trump to Shenzhen published at 09:00 GMT 09:00 GMT 
 Laura Bicker 
Reporting from Shenzhen 
 Others said they wanted to make Trump feel welcome.
 But it’s not just world leaders the people of Shenzhen are keen to meet.
 Many foreign journalists, including our BBC teams, have found themselves embraced by local people eager to say hello. It is rare for people here to meet a Western journalist as there are so few in China.
 There is also a sense of excitement in the parks and on the streets that this city of 18 million people has been chosen to host such an historic moment.
 Image source, Reuters Image caption, Shenzhen residents gathering to catch a glimpse of Trump
 Small groups of people from Shenzhen have gathered along the route of Donald Trump’s motorcade to welcome the US president.
 Security and surveillance in parts of the city have ramped up in the last few hours, in preparation for the unprecedented summit between all three of the world’s most powerful men.
 “I hope Mr Trump coming here can be a bridge between the US and China,” one young man told us as he waited on a street corner near the US president’s hotel.
 Image source, Reuters Image caption, Earlier, some residents were taking photographs as Air Force One was about to touch down in Shenzhen

 Beijing-Moscow ties 'unshaken by storms' says Xi published at 08:34 GMT 08:34 GMT 
 Image source, EPA We're getting some updates from Chinese state media on Xi's earlier meeting with Putin. The Chinese leader described relations between Beijing and Moscow as "stable as a mountain, unshaken by storms".
 The relationship between both countries has "provided greater stability and certainty to a world fraught with turmoil and upheaval", Xi said, according to China's Xinhua News Agency.
 Xi also urged both states to strengthen cooperation and explore new areas of collaboration.
 As we reported earlier, Xi and Putin largely echoed each other's remarks and hailed bilateral ties.

 Key issues to watch at Apec published at 08:16 GMT 08:16 GMT 
 The trilateral meeting: All eyes will be on Thursday's unprecedented gathering between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. 
 Trade tensions: Trump's tariffs have upended global trade order, and China has responded by choking off vital exports like rare earths. A delicate truce on the trade war is set to expire in January. 
 AI and chips: AI chips are at the centre of a heated US-China tech race. The recent Nvidia scandal has triggered scrutiny on the alleged smuggling of chips to China, which the US says is a national security issue.
 Denuclearisation: Trump said talks with Putin and Xi would cover "a lot of things including denuclearisation". But China has long been reluctant to participate in nuclear disarmament talks, citing the disparity between its arsenal and those of the US and Russia. 
 The war in Ukraine: Experts think a breakthrough is unlikely, due to a tangle of conflicting interests and the lack of Ukraine's participation. US officials have reportedly said Trump was unlikely to broach the topic with Putin and Xi. 
 The Iran war: Trump has signalled his intention to discuss the Iran war at the trilateral. Moscow and Beijing, while not formal allies of Iran, have maintained strategic partnerships with the Islamic Republic.

 What will Xi want from the US? published at 08:03 GMT 08:03 GMT 
 Osmond Chia 
Business reporter 
 Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Xi Jinping will be meeting Donald Trump for the third time this year.
 And while most experts don't expect major breakthroughs in US-China trade relations, the two nations will likely make some effort to stabilise their fragile trade truce. 
 The steep tariffs threatened by both sides have been suspended until early next year, but Washington this week imposed tougher curbs on semiconductor trade through South East Asia, which China has relied on to rent advanced AI chips. 
 Tensions between the sides have also grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang resigned following allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. 
 Xi's key goal at the Apec summit is to show that the Nvidia scandal and US mid-term results have not undermined US-China relations, Yeling Tan from the Peterson Institute for International Economics says. 
 Beijing will also want both sides to commit to cooperating and managing conflicts, Tan adds.

 Why Europe is wary of a Xi-Trump-Putin meeting published at 07:49 GMT 07:49 GMT 
 There are concerns, particularly in Europe, that the trilateral between Xi, Trump and Putin would mirror the Yalta Conference held in 1945 as World War Two drew to a close.
 Yalta, attended by then-US President Franklin D Roosevelt, former British PM Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin, was fiercely criticised for decisions that shaped the futures of smaller nations without their participation.
 Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned against holding a "Yalta 2, 3, or 4, with a redistribution of influence". He also raised fears the meeting could lead to a deal on Ukraine without Kyiv's involvement.
 Some political analysts say the US and China will have much to lose if Europe gets sidelined.
 "Moscow would certainly welcome that, but for Washington and Beijing, both of which count Europe as a large and vital economic partner, it would be a cost that is neither necessary nor worthwhile," wrote David Abramson and Evgeny Roshchin in a commentary for the Center for European Policy Analysis.
 Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Churchill (left) and Roosevelt (centre) have been criticised for capitulating to Stalin at the Yalta Conference

 Trilateral meeting will involve discussions of 'global peace' - Chinese foreign ministry published at 07:37 GMT 07:37 GMT 
 China's foreign ministry says the trilateral meeting between Xi, Trump and Putin will involve the exchange of "in-depth views" on issues related to "global peace", state media outlet Xinhua reports.
 This vague description echoes previous comments from Beijing that the three leaders would discuss "safeguarding world peace".
 Key issues loom over bilateral and trilateral ties, including trade tensions, AI, denuclearisation, and the wars in Ukraine and Iran. But what's actually going to be on the table for discussions remain unclear.

 Tarmac diplomacy: Who will welcome Trump when he arrives in China? published at 07:24 GMT 07:24 GMT 
 Ian Tang 
BBC Monitoring 
 Image source, Getty Images One detail worth watching is who will welcome Trump at the tarmac.
 Beijing's choice of Chinese official greeting the US president
would be an indication of how much they value his visit.
 During Trump's state visit to China in May, the Chinese leadership
sent Vice-President Han Zheng to welcome the US president at the tarmac.
 During Xi's state visit to the US in September, Trump took the
unusual step of greeting him personally at the tarmac.
 China would certainly want to reciprocate the gesture by sending a
high-ranking member of the Communist Party's Political Bureau to welcome Trump. But it is unlikely that Xi would go to the airport given his tight
schedule.Cai Qi, his de facto chief of staff, would be
the ideal substitute.
 Cai also received Putin this morning, so this would allow Beijing to signal that it values the US and Russian leaders' visits equally.

 Xi and Putin conclude talks after more than two hours - state media published at 07:09 GMT 07:09 GMT 
 Talks between Xi and Putin have ended after more than two hours and Putin has left the state guesthouse where the meeting was held, according to Russia's state news agency TASS.
 Among the topics the two delegations discussed were "prospects for further economic cooperation between Russia and China", TASS said.
 In a transcript of Xi's and Putin's opening remarks, published by the Kremlin, both leaders hailed their bilateral ties and pointed out that this was their third in-person meeting this year.
 Xi urged both countries to "move forward steadily and boldly, constantly unlocking the enormous potential of bilateral relations". Putin, for his part, highlighted the growth in trade between both countries and their "substantive dialogue in scientific research and innovation".

 Trump has left Philippines capital of Manila, en route to Shenzhen published at 07:06 GMT 07:06 GMT 
 Air Force One, carrying Trump, has departed the Philippines. 
 It's headed to the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, where the Apec summit is being held.
 The flight from Manila to Shenzhen is expected to take around two hours.

 Robot diplomacy on show in Shenzhen published at 07:05 GMT 07:05 GMT 
 Image source, Reuters Image caption, Leju Robot humanoid robots patrol an area outside the venue
 Along with top level global diplomacy, China is also using this summit as a chance to showcase its high tech in Shenzhen.
 Humanoid robots have staged coordinated dances, while others have been welcoming visitors and serving refreshments at venues at the event.
 The robots can be seen not just as novelties to peek delegates' interest but also Beijing flexing its leadership in physical AI and highlighting its ambitions to dominate the technology market.
